# AML Canada

> AML and regulatory compliance services in Canada. AML Canada helps money services businesses, virtual currency dealers, payment service providers and fintechs register with FINTRAC and the Bank of Canada (RPAA), build compliance programs under the PCMLTFA, run their compliance function with an outsourced compliance officer, prepare for examinations and train their staff. Operated by ComplyFactor Limited, a private consultancy not affiliated with FINTRAC or the Bank of Canada.

## Services

- [Outsourced compliance officer](https://amlcanada.ca/outsourced-compliance-officer.html): An outsourced Canadian AML compliance officer (MLRO): onboarding reviews, FINTRAC reporting, policies and risk assessments. US$1,500 per month for 10 hours.
- [MSB registration](https://amlcanada.ca/msb-registration.html): FINTRAC registration for money services businesses, foreign MSBs and virtual currency (crypto) dealers. Fixed fee US$3,500, prepared and submitted with you.
- [Compliance programs](https://amlcanada.ca/compliance-programs.html): FINTRAC compliance program documents under the PCMLTFA: policies and procedures, risk assessment, training and review plans. Fixed fee US$3,500.
- [Canadian business address](https://amlcanada.ca/canadian-address.html): A Canadian business address for foreign MSBs and companies entering Canada, for your setup, banking and partners. US$200 per month, terms agreed in writing.
- [MSB for sale](https://amlcanada.ca/msb-for-sale.html): Buy a ready-made Canadian MSB: FINTRAC-registered companies for sale now, from €28,000. Check each one on FINTRAC's registry before you pay.
- [Buy or register an MSB](https://amlcanada.ca/buy-or-register-msb-canada.html): Two ways to open an MSB in Canada: register your own with FINTRAC for US$3,500, or buy a registered company from €28,000. For founders in Canada and abroad.
- [RPAA registration](https://amlcanada.ca/rpaa-registration.html): Register as a payment service provider (PSP) with the Bank of Canada under the RPAA. Fixed fee US$3,500, plus the Bank's own application fee.
- [RPAA compliance program](https://amlcanada.ca/rpaa-compliance-program.html): RPAA frameworks for PSPs: governance, risk registers, incident response, third parties, safeguarding, cyber and continuity, annual reports. Fixed fee US$3,500.
- [Effectiveness reviews](https://amlcanada.ca/effectiveness-reviews.html): The FINTRAC two-year effectiveness review, often called an AML audit: your policies, risk assessment and training tested, with written findings.
- [Training](https://amlcanada.ca/training.html): FINTRAC AML training in Canada for MSB front-line staff, compliance teams and senior management, built to meet FINTRAC's training requirement.
- [Company incorporation](https://amlcanada.ca/incorporation-canada.html): Incorporate a Canadian company, federally or in Ontario, usually within 24 hours. Fixed fee US$1,500, ready for FINTRAC or RPAA registration.
- [Apostille & notarization](https://amlcanada.ca/apostille-notarization-canada.html): Apostille and notarization of Canadian corporate documents for foreign banks, payment partners and regulators, with a licensed Ontario partner notary.
- [FINTRAC reporting software](https://amlcanada.ca/fintrac-reporting-software.html): FINTRAC reporting software for STRs, LCTRs, EFTRs, LVCTRs and CDRs: data import, 24-hour rule checks, validation, maker-checker approval and API submission.
- [Sell your MSB](https://amlcanada.ca/sell-your-msb.html): Sell your MSB in Canada. We check your FINTRAC-registered company, match it with a buyer, and handle the share sale and the FINTRAC updates.

## Guides

- [Commissioner of oaths vs notary public: what each can do in Ontario](https://amlcanada.ca/commissioner-of-oaths-vs-notary-public.html): Commissioner of oaths vs notary public comes down to powers. In Ontario, a commissioner for taking affidavits can administer oaths and take affidavits, declarations and affirmations. A notary public can do all of that and can also witness and attest signatures and certify true copies, which matters for documents going abroad.
- [Certified true copy in Canada: who can certify and when you need a notary](https://amlcanada.ca/certified-true-copy-canada.html): A certified true copy is a photocopy that an authorized person has compared with the original and marked as a true copy. Canada has no single list of who may certify one. IRCC, Service Canada and Public Safety Canada each publish their own list, the Passport Program certifies passport copies itself, and Global Affairs Canada accepts notary-certified copies for authentication. In practice, a copy going abroad with an apostille usually needs a notary.
- [Apostille in BC: how to get a British Columbia apostille](https://amlcanada.ca/apostille-british-columbia.html): An apostille in BC comes from the B.C. Authentication Program in Victoria, which authenticates British Columbia public documents for use outside Canada. As of 26 November 2026 the fee is CA$20 per document, requests go by mail or courier only, and the published processing time is 2 to 4 weeks plus mail time.
- [How to get an apostille in Alberta](https://amlcanada.ca/apostille-alberta.html): To get an apostille in Alberta, you mail or courier your documents to Official Documents and Appointments in Edmonton with a request form and an online payment receipt. As of 26 November 2026, Alberta charges CA$25 per document, offers no walk-in service and asks you to allow at least 7 to 10 business days.
- [How to get an apostille in Quebec (2026 guide)](https://amlcanada.ca/apostille-quebec.html): An apostille in Quebec is issued by the Ministère de la Justice du Québec for documents issued in Quebec, and requests go in by mail. As of 26 November 2026 the fee is CA$66.50 per document. Quebec issues its apostilles in French only.
- [How to get an apostille in Ontario](https://amlcanada.ca/apostille-ontario.html): An Ontario apostille is issued by Official Documents Services (ODS), the provincial office that authenticates documents for use outside Canada. ODS handles documents issued in Ontario and documents notarized by an Ontario notary public. Original federal documents go to Global Affairs Canada.
- [Apostille vs notary in Canada: what each step does and who does it](https://amlcanada.ca/apostille-vs-notarization-canada.html): The apostille vs notary question comes down to who signs what. A notary public witnesses a signature, takes an oath or certifies a copy. An apostille is a certificate from a government competent authority that confirms that signature and seal, so the document can be used in another Apostille Convention country.
- [MSB bank account in Canada: what a bank must check and what to have ready](https://amlcanada.ca/msb-bank-account-canada.html): An MSB bank account in Canada depends on the bank's own legal duties: under the PCMLTFA, a bank must verify your business and the people who give instructions on the account, collect your ownership information and take reasonable measures to confirm it, record why you want the account, assess your risk and keep monitoring you. FINTRAC registration doesn't guarantee an account, and each bank makes its own decision. Below are the rules behind the bank's questions, as of 25 November 2026, and a checklist of what to have ready.
- [Auditor General audit of FINTRAC: what MSBs should know](https://amlcanada.ca/auditor-general-fintrac-audit-2026-msb-lessons.html): The Auditor General of Canada tabled an audit of FINTRAC on 29 October 2026 that found weak compliance oversight, slow financial intelligence and about 2,500 money services business registration requests still waiting to be processed. FINTRAC agreed with every recommendation. This post sets out the findings that affect MSBs and the checks they point to.
- [FINTRAC's 2025-26 annual report: what the supervision figures mean for MSBs](https://amlcanada.ca/fintrac-annual-report-2025-26-msb-supervision.html): FINTRAC published its 2025-26 annual report on 26 October 2026. In the year to 31 March 2026, money services businesses received more than 55% of its assessment activity, 433 targeted examinations and information demands, and 82 registration revocations. This post sets out the supervision and enforcement figures that matter to MSBs and the compliance checks they point to.
- [OFAC sanctions eight Canadian MSBs: what money services businesses should check](https://amlcanada.ca/ofac-sanctions-canadian-msbs-iran-fintrac.html): On 6 November 2026, the US Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) designated eight money services businesses based in Canada under its Iran sanctions, and FINTRAC said it coordinated with OFAC and FinCEN on the action. For Canadian MSBs, it is a reason to recheck sanctions screening and how Iran-connected transactions are identified and reported.
- [RPAA business continuity plan: recovery and testing for PSPs](https://amlcanada.ca/rpaa-business-continuity-testing.html): An RPAA business continuity plan is the recovery part of the risk management and incident response framework every payment service provider must keep. The regulations require a response and recovery plan, measurable reliability targets and a testing methodology with a record of each test. This guide covers what the plan contains, how and how often to test it, and what to keep.
- [Outsourcing RPAA compliance: what a PSP can hand over and what it keeps](https://amlcanada.ca/rpaa-outsourcing-risk-management-psp.html): A payment service provider can outsource RPAA compliance work, such as writing its risk management and incident response framework, assessing risks and drafting notices, to an outside risk officer or adviser. The PSP keeps the legal duty: approval by its senior officer and board, the notices and filings, the records and the oversight of anyone it hands work to.
- [How to choose an outsourced compliance officer in Canada](https://amlcanada.ca/choosing-outsourced-compliance-officer-canada.html): How to choose an outsourced compliance officer comes down to three checks: what the provider will do for your FINTRAC program, what the written agreement gives them in authority and access, and whether anything they claim conflicts with FINTRAC's rules. This checklist is for a FINTRAC-regulated business that has already decided to outsource the role.
- [FINTRAC transaction monitoring requirements: ongoing monitoring for MSBs](https://amlcanada.ca/fintrac-ongoing-monitoring-transaction-monitoring.html): FINTRAC transaction monitoring requirements for an MSB start with section 123.1 of the Regulations: once you have a business relationship with a client, you must monitor it periodically, at a frequency set by your risk assessment, to detect suspicious transactions and keep client information current. The rules, thresholds and alert reviews that put this into practice come from FINTRAC's guidance and examination manual, and this guide marks which parts are law, guidance or practice.
- [KYC checklist for MSBs in Canada: what an onboarding file needs before review](https://amlcanada.ca/msb-onboarding-file-review-checklist.html): A KYC checklist for MSBs in Canada lists what a client onboarding file needs before the compliance officer can decide on it: verified identity, beneficial ownership, the politically exposed person and third party determinations, the sanctions check, the purpose of the relationship and a risk rating. Each item below is tied to its section of the Regulations or to FINTRAC guidance, as of 19 November 2026.
- [The second line of defence in AML: how the three lines map to FINTRAC rules](https://amlcanada.ca/second-line-of-defence-aml-canada.html): The second line of defence in AML is the compliance function that sets the rules, checks the operations team's work and decides on the files the team escalates. The term comes from the three lines of defence, a widely used governance model. FINTRAC's compliance program guidance and assessment manual don't use it, so this guide maps each line onto what the law requires of an MSB.
- [How does an outsourced compliance officer work?](https://amlcanada.ca/outsourced-compliance-officer-how-it-works.html): An outsourced compliance officer works through escalation. Your business appoints an outside professional as the person responsible for implementing its compliance program, and your operations team runs onboarding and monitoring day to day, escalating files to that person for a compliance decision. Your business stays the reporting entity throughout, and this guide shows how the work divides.
- [How to incorporate in Canada as a non-resident](https://amlcanada.ca/incorporate-in-canada-non-resident.html): You can incorporate in Canada as a non-resident, and you don't need to live in Canada or hold Canadian citizenship to own the company. The jurisdictions differ on who can sit on the board: a federal corporation needs resident Canadian directors, and Ontario, British Columbia and Alberta have no director residency rule.
- [FINTRAC training requirements: the program, the plan and the records](https://amlcanada.ca/fintrac-training-requirements.html): FINTRAC training requirements come from section 156 of the Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Regulations. If anyone works or acts for you, you need a written, ongoing compliance training program and a documented plan for delivering it. Neither the Regulations nor FINTRAC fix how often you train, so your plan sets the frequency and your records should show you kept to it.
- [Is there a payment service provider licence in Canada?](https://amlcanada.ca/psp-licence-canada.html): There is no payment service provider licence in Canada. A PSP covered by the Retail Payment Activities Act registers with the Bank of Canada, which lists it on a public registry and says it does not license or endorse PSPs. Depending on your business, FINTRAC registration, a Quebec licence or Payments Canada membership may also apply.
- [FINTRAC risk assessment for MSBs: the rules and a worked example](https://amlcanada.ca/fintrac-risk-assessment-msb.html): A FINTRAC risk assessment for MSBs is the written assessment of how your clients, services, delivery channels and locations could expose you to money laundering or terrorist financing. Section 156 of the Regulations lists the factors, and FINTRAC's guidance describes a method. Below, each factor is matched to its legal source and to the evidence an examiner may ask to see.
- [How to check FINTRAC MSB registration](https://amlcanada.ca/check-fintrac-msb-registration.html): To check FINTRAC MSB registration, search the business's legal name, operating name or registration number in FINTRAC's Money Services Business Registry and confirm the status reads Registered. Then match the name, number, website and services on the entry to the business you are dealing with. A listing confirms registration only, because FINTRAC does not license or endorse money services businesses.
- [FINTRAC MSB registration renewal: how and when to renew](https://amlcanada.ca/msb-registration-renewal-canada.html): FINTRAC MSB registration renewal is due every two years under section 11.19 of the Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act, and FINTRAC says you must renew before the expiry date. A renewal filed in time keeps you Registered while FINTRAC processes it. This guide covers the dates, the information to refresh and the 30-day deadlines that run alongside renewal.
- [FINTRAC compliance officer requirements, with MSB specifics](https://amlcanada.ca/msb-compliance-officer-requirements-canada.html): The core FINTRAC compliance officer requirement is short: every business FINTRAC regulates must appoint a person responsible for implementing its compliance program. Most of what people call requirements, such as seniority, independence and knowledge, comes from FINTRAC's guidance, and this guide marks which is which, using money services businesses (MSBs) as the example.
- [Real-Time Rail access for PSPs and the RPAA digital wallet amendment](https://amlcanada.ca/real-time-rail-rpaa-digital-wallets.html): Real-Time Rail access is now open to payment service providers (PSPs) registered under the RPAA, through Payments Canada membership, and Payments Canada targets the system's launch for Q4 2026. Separately, Bill C-15 adds a payment function for tokenized payment instruments and private keys, which, as of 3 November 2026, isn't in force.
- [PSP insolvency: what happens to end-user funds in Canada](https://amlcanada.ca/psp-insolvency-end-user-funds-canada.html): In a PSP insolvency in Canada, the end-user funds a payment service provider holds are meant to be paid to end users as soon as feasible, because section 20 of the RPAA requires those funds to be held in trust or covered by insurance or a guarantee. Whether that works depends on the provider's ledger, its shortfall checks and its written procedures for returning funds.
- [How to check Bank of Canada PSP registration](https://amlcanada.ca/check-bank-of-canada-psp-registration.html): To check Bank of Canada PSP registration, search the company's legal or trade name in the Bank's Registry of payment service providers, then check its list of applicants, refused or revoked list and enforcement decisions. As of 3 November 2026, the registry listed 1,789 PSPs. A listing confirms registration only, because the Bank does not license or endorse PSPs.
- [How to complete Section 4 of the RPAA annual report](https://amlcanada.ca/rpaa-annual-report-section-4-metrics.html): Section 4 of the RPAA annual report collects your ubiquity and interconnectedness metrics: end-user funds held, the monthly number and value of electronic funds transfers, and how many end users and other PSPs you served. Each figure is split by currency and between all end users and end users in Canada. This guide covers each question, the Bank of Canada's counting rules and the checks to run before the March 31, 2027 deadline.
- [The RPAA trust account legal opinion: what the Bank of Canada asks for](https://amlcanada.ca/rpaa-safeguarding-legal-opinion-trust-account.html): The RPAA trust account legal opinion is a written opinion the Bank of Canada asks for when it assesses a payment service provider (PSP) that holds end-user funds in trust. As of 3 November 2026, the Bank's FAQ and self-assessment tool say it must show a valid express trust under common law or the Civil Code of Québec, set out the risks to that trust, and deal with any interest, dividends or capital gains the PSP receives. A lawyer must prepare it, and this guide is not legal advice.
- [PSP Connect: a practical guide for payment service providers](https://amlcanada.ca/psp-connect-guide.html): PSP Connect is the Bank of Canada's online portal where payment service providers register, file their RPAA reports and notices, and receive messages from supervisors. As of 3 November 2026, this guide explains who can use your account, how messages and the primary contact work, what you file there and by when, and where to go when the portal misbehaves.
- [Bank of Canada PSP supervision update, 2 November 2026: what PSPs heard](https://amlcanada.ca/bank-of-canada-psp-supervision-update-november-2026.html): At its Bank of Canada PSP supervision update on 2 November 2026, the Bank told payment service providers (PSPs) that it expects full compliance with the Retail Payment Activities Act (RPAA) now, after its first year of supervision. Staff covered assessments, safeguarding, enforcement, AI risk, PSP Connect, annual reporting, cost recovery and policy, then answered 14 audience questions.
- [FINTRAC penalizes Necosmart $693,742.50: what virtual currency MSBs can learn](https://amlcanada.ca/fintrac-penalty-necosmart-virtual-currency-msb.html): FINTRAC imposed a $693,742.50 administrative monetary penalty on 13010431 Canada Inc., also operating as Necosmart, a money services business in Edmonton, Alberta, for 5 violations found during a compliance examination. Two of the violations involve controls the business had written down but did not carry out.
- [The RPAA compliance frameworks a PSP needs](https://amlcanada.ca/rpaa-compliance-frameworks.html): Every payment service provider needs a written risk management and incident response framework, and one that holds end-user funds also needs a safeguarding-of-funds framework. Third parties, agents and the senior officer's role are built into those two documents. Record keeping rules cover both, and the annual report, change notices and incident notices draw on them.
- [FINTRAC revoked your MSB registration: a response plan](https://amlcanada.ca/fintrac-revocation-response-plan.html): A revoked registration means the business can't offer the money services it was registered for. You have 30 days from receiving the decision to ask FINTRAC's Director to review it. Stop the registered services straight away, because the Act doesn't pause a revocation while a review runs.
- [Crypto custody in Canada: the rules and custody models compared](https://amlcanada.ca/crypto-custody-canada.html): Canada has no single crypto custody licence. A platform that holds client crypto is expected to register with securities regulators. Under CSA pre-registration undertakings, which broadly match the terms registered platforms work under, client crypto is held in trust, mostly with an acceptable third-party custodian. Exchanging or transferring crypto for clients means FINTRAC registration. The Bank of Canada comes in where fiat payments are involved and, once the Stablecoin Act is in force, for stablecoin issuers.
- [Ontario vs B.C. MSB registration: which province suits a crypto startup?](https://amlcanada.ca/ontario-vs-bc-msb-registration.html): Today there's no MSB difference between the two provinces. A money services business in Ontario or British Columbia registers with FINTRAC and nobody else, because B.C.'s Money Services Businesses Act has been passed but isn't in force. That should change: B.C. plans to start provincial registration, and Ontario has no equivalent law.
- [RPAA incident reporting and the 48-hour rule](https://amlcanada.ca/rpaa-incident-reporting.html): When a payment service provider becomes aware of an incident with a material impact, it must notify the Bank of Canada and the affected end users, payment service providers and clearing houses without delay. The Bank expects the first notice no later than 48 hours after the provider decides the incident is material.
- [RPAA vs FINTRAC MSB registration: do you need both?](https://amlcanada.ca/rpaa-vs-fintrac-msb-registration.html): Payment service providers register with the Bank of Canada under the RPAA. Money services businesses register with FINTRAC under the PCMLTFA. Many payment businesses are both, and the two registrations are linked: the Bank shares your application with FINTRAC and can refuse it based on what FINTRAC reports.
- [The RPAA annual report for payment service providers](https://amlcanada.ca/rpaa-annual-report.html): Every payment service provider that performs retail payment activities in a calendar year must file an annual report with the Bank of Canada by March 31 of the following year. It covers your risk management and incident response framework, safeguarding, activity metrics and financial results.
- [Who must register as a PSP under the RPAA?](https://amlcanada.ca/who-must-register-psp-rpaa.html): You must register with the Bank of Canada if you perform a payment function as a business in its own right, for electronic transfers in Canadian or foreign currency, with a link to Canada, and no exclusion applies. This guide shows how the Bank applies each part of that test to real business models.
- [Apostilling Canadian corporate documents for foreign banks and regulators](https://amlcanada.ca/apostille-corporate-documents-canada.html): Foreign banks, payment partners and regulators often want Canadian corporate documents with an apostille. Some government certificates can go straight to the authority. Most corporate records must be notarized first.
- [How to get an apostille in Canada (2026 guide)](https://amlcanada.ca/apostille-canada-guide.html): Since January 11, 2024, Canadian public documents going to Apostille Convention countries get an apostille. Who issues it depends on where the document was issued or notarized: Global Affairs Canada, or one of five provinces.
- [The travel rule and ministerial directives: what Canadian MSBs must do](https://amlcanada.ca/fintrac-travel-rule-ministerial-directives.html): Canada's travel rule requires money services businesses to send originator and beneficiary information with funds and virtual currency transfers, and to check it arrives with transfers they receive. Ministerial directives add stricter measures for transactions connected to Russia, Iran and North Korea.
- [FINTRAC administrative monetary penalties (AMPs) explained](https://amlcanada.ca/fintrac-penalties-amps.html): FINTRAC can impose administrative monetary penalties for breaches of the anti-money laundering law. Amendments in force since March 26, 2026 raised the maximum amounts up to 40 times and added compliance agreements and compliance orders.
- [MSB registration denied, revoked or expired: what happens and what to do](https://amlcanada.ca/msb-registration-refused-revoked.html): FINTRAC can deny an MSB application or revoke a registration for a short list of reasons set out in the Act. A registration that isn't renewed expires. Each outcome has its own deadlines, and operating without a valid registration is an offence.
- [Can you use a virtual office for FINTRAC MSB registration?](https://amlcanada.ca/virtual-office-msb-registration.html): FINTRAC's published guidance doesn't say whether a virtual office is acceptable. It does say what counts as a place of business in Canada, what the registration asks about your addresses, and that FINTRAC can check the information you give it.
- [RPAA safeguarding of end-user funds](https://amlcanada.ca/rpaa-safeguarding-end-user-funds.html): Since September 8, 2025, a payment service provider that holds funds for its users must safeguard them, either in trust in a trust account or in a segregated account backed by insurance or a guarantee. It also needs a written safeguarding framework and an independent review at least every three years.
- [FINTRAC compliance program requirements](https://amlcanada.ca/fintrac-compliance-program-requirements.html): Every business FINTRAC regulates must establish and implement a compliance program. It has five parts: a compliance officer, written policies and procedures, a risk assessment, an ongoing training program and plan, and a review of the program at least every two years.
- [The first 90 days of AML compliance after FINTRAC registration](https://amlcanada.ca/first-90-days-aml-compliance-canada.html): Once a money services business in Canada is registered with FINTRAC, its obligations apply from the day it starts operating. This guide sets out a practical order for the first three months and the legal deadlines to put in your diary.
- [FINTRAC MSB change of ownership: what to report and when](https://amlcanada.ca/fintrac-msb-change-of-ownership.html): When a registered money services business changes hands, its registration stays with the company, but FINTRAC has to be told about the changes within 30 days.
- [Buying a registered MSB company: what should come with it and which claims to question](https://amlcanada.ca/ready-made-msb-company-canada.html): A ready-made MSB is a Canadian company that's already registered with FINTRAC, sold through a share purchase. Here's what should come with one, and which sales claims don't hold up.
- [Is there an MSB licence in Canada?](https://amlcanada.ca/msb-licence-canada.html): People search for a Canadian "MSB licence". What FINTRAC actually gives a money services business is a registration, and the difference matters when you buy, bank or advertise one.
- [Outsourced or in-house compliance officer?](https://amlcanada.ca/outsourced-vs-in-house-compliance-officer.html): Every business FINTRAC regulates needs a compliance officer. You can appoint the owner or a manager, hire someone, or outsource the role, and FINTRAC's expectations are the same in each case.
- [MSB due diligence: what to check before you buy](https://amlcanada.ca/buying-an-msb-canada.html): Buying a company that's already registered with FINTRAC as a money services business needs the same care as any acquisition, plus checks specific to FINTRAC and, for payment businesses, the Bank of Canada.
- [Preparing for a FINTRAC examination](https://amlcanada.ca/fintrac-examination-preparation.html): A FINTRAC examination usually starts with a call to your compliance officer and a letter asking for documents. Examinations can be done remotely or on site, and findings can lead to follow-up or a penalty.
- [The two-year effectiveness review: a checklist](https://amlcanada.ca/fintrac-effectiveness-review-checklist.html): FINTRAC requires every reporting entity to review its compliance program at least every two years. The review should test how the program works in practice as well as what's written down.
- [Registering a crypto business with FINTRAC](https://amlcanada.ca/crypto-registration-canada.html): Crypto exchanges and virtual currency dealers register with FINTRAC as money services businesses, whether they're based in Canada or serve Canadians from abroad.
- [How to apply for RPAA registration with the Bank of Canada](https://amlcanada.ca/rpaa-registration-guide.html): Payment service providers covered by the Retail Payment Activities Act (RPAA) apply to the Bank of Canada online, through PSP Connect. Since 8 September 2025, a new applicant can't start retail payment activities until the Bank registers it.
- [FINTRAC reporting for MSBs: which report, and when](https://amlcanada.ca/fintrac-reporting-requirements.html): Money services businesses report suspicious transactions, large cash, international transfers, large virtual currency receipts and listed person property to FINTRAC. Each report has its own trigger and deadline.
- [Foreign MSB registration in Canada](https://amlcanada.ca/foreign-msb-registration-canada.html): A business with no office in Canada may still have to register with FINTRAC. It does if it directs and provides money services to people or entities in Canada.
- [How much does MSB registration cost in Canada?](https://amlcanada.ca/msb-registration-cost-canada.html): FINTRAC doesn't charge a fee to register a money services business. The costs come from criminal record checks, translations, documents and the compliance program you need to operate.
- [How to apply to FINTRAC as an MSB: 6 steps](https://amlcanada.ca/how-to-register-msb-canada.html): A money services business must register with FINTRAC before it starts operating, and renew every two years. FINTRAC doesn't charge a fee, and it says the majority of complete applications are processed within three months.
